passage: Rain hammered the tarpaulin over the colony's festival ground and everyone squeezed under it to sing. Mohit, eight, ducked in among the other children, dripping. A man holding a steel ladle stepped in front of him. "Not you. Your family isn't one of ours." The singing carried on behind the man's back. Mohit's ears burned and water ran down his neck. He did not understand what he had done. He stood at the edge in the rain until his Masi Sudha arrived with an umbrella and saw his face. He told her in a rush. She put her arm around him. "That was not because of anything you did. Come, I'm going to speak to the organisers."

qa.q: What was the man in front of Mohit holding?
qa.a: He was holding a steel ladle.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling and thinking as he stood at the edge in the rain?
qa.a: He was hurt and confused: his ears burned and he did not understand what he had done.

qa.q: Who could Mohit tell, and what does that do for him?
qa.a: He can tell a trusted adult like Masi Sudha, who reassures him it was not because of anything he did and goes to speak up for him 🤍.

qa.q: How might Masi Sudha see what happened?
qa.a: As unfair to a child: she put her arm around him and went to speak to the organisers.

grounding: Illustrates a child told he cannot join a community gathering because of who his family is, hurt and confused, and turning to a trusted adult.

passage: At the Ganesh festival in our building compound last year, the older kids were taking turns to carry the small palki. I'm Mohit. When I stepped up, one of the organisers looked at the surname on my name tag and said, 'Not you. This is only for our people.' I didn't even understand what he meant. My face went hot, and I stood at the back, confused, trying not to cry. I told Lakshmi Aunty from the second floor, who was running the prasad table. She put down her ladle, took my hand and walked straight to the organiser. 'Every child here can carry it,' she said firmly. The pujari nodded. 'God does not shut out children.' I carried the palki in the next round. Aunty told me it was never my fault.

qa.q: What was Mohit told at the palki?
qa.a: 'Not you. This is only for our people.'

qa.q: How did Mohit feel standing at the back?
qa.a: Hurt and confused, face hot, trying not to cry.

qa.q: What did Mohit do, and how did the adult respond?
qa.a: Told Lakshmi Aunty, who went straight to the organiser, said every child can carry the palki, and told Mohit it was never Mohit's fault.

qa.q: How did the pujari see the organiser's rule?
qa.a: As wrong; the pujari said God does not shut out children.

grounding: A child shut out of a festival ritual because of their family name tells a trusted adult, who restores their place at once.

passage:
Note by Tanuja D'Costa, Sunday school coordinator, after the Christmas party.
Vidya, aged nine, came with her neighbours, the Fernandes family. When the children lined up for the nativity play, one of our volunteers told her, 'You can't be in it. You're not one of us.' I saw Vidya's face crumple; she went and sat under the stairs, hugging her knees. Mrs Fernandes found her and brought her to me straight away. I knelt beside Vidya and told her clearly that it was not her fault and that no child is shut out here. I gave her the part of a star, and she shone at it, holding up her tinsel. I have spoken to the volunteer, and this evening I phoned Vidya's mother to explain and apologise.

qa.q: Where did Vidya go after being told she couldn't join?
qa.a: Under the stairs, hugging her knees.

qa.q: What did Vidya's crumpling face show?
qa.a: She felt hurt and confused at being shut out.

qa.q: What did the coordinator do the same day?
qa.a: Told Vidya it wasn't her fault, gave her the star part, spoke to the volunteer and phoned her mother to apologise.

qa.q: How might Mrs Fernandes have felt finding Vidya under the stairs?
qa.a: Upset and protective, which is why she brought Vidya to the coordinator straight away.

grounding: A coordinator's note records a visiting girl told she cannot join a church play, and adults at once including her and correcting the volunteer.
